cases.name: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Jorge Reyes had a recurring fever with chills for five days that home medicine did not relieve. On January 8, 1987 his wife brought him to the Mercy Community Clinic. Dr. Marlyn Rico examined him and, since typhoid fever was common in the area at the time (the clinic was seeing 15 to 20 cases a month), ordered a Widal Test, which came out positive. Dr. Marvie Blanes, who took over, ordered a compatibility test with the antibiotic chloromycetin, saw no adverse reaction, and had two 500-milligram doses given about three hours apart. Past midnight Jorge's temperature rose to 41°C and he had chills, vomiting and convulsions. Emergency measures failed, and he died at about 2:00 a.m., some ten hours after admission. His widow and children sued the hospital, its directress and the two doctors for damages, claiming he died not of typhoid but because chloromycetin was wrongly given. Their pathologist, who did the autopsy without opening the skull, said Jorge did not die of typhoid. Two specialists for the doctors said the diagnosis and the drug were correct and the autopsy was incomplete. The trial court and the Court of Appeals dismissed the complaint.
cases.issue: (1) Does the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur apply, so that no expert testimony is needed to prove the doctors' negligence? (2) Did the heirs prove specific acts of negligence by the doctors? (3) Are doctors, like common carriers, bound to observe extraordinary diligence?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition and affirmed the dismissal. (1) Res ipsa loquitur does not apply. A patient who had been sick with fever and chills for five days, unrelieved by medicine, dying a few hours after admission is not unusual or extraordinary; the alleged lack of care was not apparent to a layman, and the doctrine cannot apply to a suit that questions the merits of a diagnosis or of a scientific treatment. Expert testimony was therefore needed. (2) The heirs' only witness was a pathologist who was not a specialist in infectious diseases, had never autopsied a typhoid victim and had seen only about three typhoid cases, so his opinion was properly discarded. The defense experts showed that the Widal Test was a standard test, that the diagnosis was reasonable given the history and the local outbreak, that chloromycetin was the drug of choice, and that the dosage was within accepted limits. Doctors are only required to perform standard tests and procedures; they cannot be required to predict every reaction to a drug. (3) Extraordinary diligence is peculiar to common carriers. The standard for doctors is the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians.
cases.keyDoctrine: Medical malpractice is the failure of a physician to apply the degree of care and skill ordinarily employed by the profession generally under similar conditions. Its four elements are duty, breach, injury and proximate causation, and expert testimony is usually needed to prove them. Res ipsa loquitur, which dispenses with expert testimony, applies only where a layman can tell from common knowledge that the result would not have happened with due care; it does not apply to the merits of a diagnosis or a scientific treatment. Doctors owe the reasonable average merit of ordinarily good physicians, not the extraordinary diligence of common carriers.

cases.name: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Roy Alfonso Santiago, Jr., a young boy, was hit by a taxicab and rushed to the emergency room of the Manila Doctors Hospital. Dr. Emmanuel Jarcia, Jr. and Dr. Marilou Bastan, junior residents in general surgery, attended to him. Only his ankle was X-rayed, and Dr. Jarcia read it as showing no fracture. When his mother, a nurse, asked for an X-ray up to the knee because the boy complained of pain from the ankle to the middle of the leg, Dr. Bastan said there was no need since only the ankle had been run over, and the doctors assured her that all was well. Eleven days later the boy had fever, a swollen right leg and a misaligned foot; a new X-ray showed a fracture of the middle of the tibia. The two doctors were charged with reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries. The trial court convicted them of simple imprudence, and the Court of Appeals affirmed, applying res ipsa loquitur.
cases.issue: (1) Does res ipsa loquitur apply to the case? (2) Are the doctors criminally liable for the boy's injuries, and if not, are they civilly liable?
cases.ruling: The Court partly granted the petition. (1) Res ipsa loquitur did not apply. The circumstances that caused the injury and the tests needed to find its extent were not under the exclusive control of the two doctors, who were mere residents attending in the emergency room, and whether they used the required skill and care is generally a matter for expert opinion, not the assumptions of a layman like the mother. The doctrine is only a mode of proof, invoked when direct evidence is absent and not readily available. (2) The doctors were negligent: they did not examine the boy thoroughly, and if they could not, they should have referred him to another doctor instead of assuring the mother that everything was all right. But there was no precise evidence that the delay prolonged the pain or aggravated the injury, so guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and they were acquitted. Since civil liability needs only a preponderance of evidence, they were held civilly liable for ₱3,850 actual damages, ₱100,000 moral damages and ₱50,000 exemplary damages. They could not shift the blame to the taxi driver, even if the accident was the direct cause of the fracture. Their claim that there was no physician-patient relationship, because they merely passed by the emergency room on the way to lunch, was raised for the first time on appeal, and in any case such a relationship existed once they examined the boy and assured his mother.
cases.keyDoctrine: Res ipsa loquitur is not a rule of substantive law but a mode of proof, available only when direct evidence is absent and not readily available, and only if the instrumentality was under the defendant's exclusive control. A doctor who examines a patient in the emergency room enters into a physician-patient relationship. A doctor acquitted of reckless imprudence for lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt may still be civilly liable on a preponderance of evidence, and cannot escape liability by pointing to the person who caused the original injury.

cases.name: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Dr. Jaime T. Cruz went to St. Luke's Medical Center for a check-up in May 2003 and underwent a gastroscopy and colonoscopy performed by Dr. Felicisimo V. Agas, Jr. After the procedure he felt dizzy, had difficulty breathing, severe abdominal pain, and collapsed. He was found to have internal bleeding and underwent emergency surgery, in which 6 to 8 inches of his colon, which had a partial tear of the colonic wall, were removed. He filed a complaint for serious physical injuries through reckless imprudence and medical malpractice against Dr. Agas. Dr. Agas explained, with supporting affidavits and a certification of the hospital's ethics committee, that the bleeding came from a tear in the serosa (the outermost layer of the colon) caused by marked adhesions and the twisted shape of the patient's sigmoid colon, a condition that no test can detect before such a procedure and that the colonoscope, which passes only through the inside of the colon, could not reach. The prosecutor dismissed the complaint for lack of probable cause; the Secretary of Justice and the Court of Appeals upheld the dismissal.
cases.issue: Was the Court of Appeals correct in upholding the finding that there was no probable cause to charge Dr. Agas, because his negligence was not shown?
cases.ruling: The Court denied the petition. Courts do not interfere with the executive determination of probable cause in the absence of grave abuse of discretion, and none was shown. In a medical negligence case the patient must prove duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. Dr. Cruz showed an injury, but not the particular negligent act or omission of Dr. Agas that caused it, nor an inexcusable lack of precaution. Res ipsa loquitur did not apply: the alleged negligence was not apparent to a layman, and Dr. Agas explained that the bleeding came from an abnormal condition of the patient's colon beyond his control, which needed expert opinion to connect to the colonoscopy. Dr. Cruz did not rebut that explanation.
cases.keyDoctrine: Res ipsa loquitur means the thing speaks for itself: the occurrence of an injury, with its circumstances, may raise a presumption of negligence. Its requisites are the occurrence of an injury, control and management of the thing that caused it by the defendant, an occurrence that would not happen in the ordinary course of things with proper care, and the absence of explanation by the defendant; control and management is the most instrumental. It does not apply where the defendant explains the injury by a cause beyond his control, or where the connection between the injury and the procedure needs expert opinion.

cases.name: Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In April 1984 Dr. Miguel Ampil operated on Natividad Agana at the Medical City General Hospital, owned by Professional Services, Inc. (PSI), for cancer of the sigmoid. Finding that the cancer had spread to her left ovary, he called in Dr. Juan Fuentes, with her husband's consent, to perform a hysterectomy. Dr. Fuentes did so, showed his work to Dr. Ampil, and left. Dr. Ampil completed the operation and closed the incision, although the nurses recorded "sponge count lacking 2" and that a search had been done to no avail. Natividad later suffered severe pain, which both doctors told her was a natural consequence of the surgery. Months later her daughter found a piece of gauze protruding from her vagina; Dr. Ampil pulled it out by hand and assured her the pain would go away. Another foul-smelling gauze was later found, which had badly infected her and caused a recto-vaginal fistula, requiring another operation. Natividad and her husband sued PSI, Dr. Ampil and Dr. Fuentes for damages. The trial court held all three liable; the Court of Appeals dismissed the case against Dr. Fuentes and held Dr. Ampil and PSI liable, with Dr. Ampil to reimburse PSI.
cases.issue: (1) Is Dr. Ampil liable for negligence and malpractice? (2) Should Dr. Fuentes also be liable under res ipsa loquitur? (3) Is PSI, the hospital, liable for Dr. Ampil's negligence?
cases.ruling: The Court denied all three petitions. (1) Dr. Ampil was liable. Leaving sponges in the wound after the incision is closed is at least prima facie negligence by the operating surgeon. Even if an emergency forces a surgeon to leave a sponge, he has the legal duty to tell the patient within a reasonable time. Dr. Ampil closed the incision despite the nurses' report, did not tell Natividad, and misled her about her pain, so his negligence ripened into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving his patient. (2) Dr. Fuentes was not liable: under the Captain of the Ship rule the lead surgeon, Dr. Ampil, was in complete charge, and it was his order to close the incision that caused the injury, so the requisite of control and management was missing as to Dr. Fuentes. (3) PSI was liable: by listing Dr. Ampil and Dr. Fuentes in its lobby directory as its accredited physicians, it held them out as its agents (apparent authority), and it was directly liable for its own corporate negligence in not investigating the nurses' report of the missing gauzes. Having failed to prove the diligence of a good father of a family in accrediting and supervising Dr. Ampil, it was solidarily liable with him. (On a second motion for reconsideration, the Court en banc in 2010 kept PSI liable on apparent authority and, for this case only, corporate negligence, but not on an employer-employee relationship; see the 2010 resolution.)
cases.keyDoctrine: Leaving a sponge or other foreign object in a patient after the incision is closed is at least prima facie negligence of the operating surgeon, who must also inform the patient within a reasonable time if he had to leave it. Under the Captain of the Ship rule the operating surgeon is in complete charge of the operating room. A hospital may be liable for a doctor's negligence under apparent authority (holding the doctor out as its agent, on which the patient reasonably relies) and directly for its own corporate negligence, such as failing to supervise those who practice within its walls.

cases.name: Professional Services, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and Agana (Resolution)
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: In its 2007 decision the Court held Professional Services, Inc. (PSI), owner of the Medical City General Hospital, liable together with Dr. Miguel Ampil for the two gauzes left inside Natividad Agana after surgery. It based PSI's liability on an employer-employee relationship (following Ramos v. Court of Appeals, 1999), on apparent authority, and on corporate negligence. PSI filed a second motion for reconsideration, and other private hospitals and their association intervened, warning that the ruling would burden private hospitals and raise the cost of health care. The Court en banc heard oral arguments on one question: whether a hospital may be held liable for the negligence of physicians-consultants allowed to practice in its premises.
cases.issue: Is PSI liable for the negligence of Dr. Ampil, a consultant practicing in its hospital, and on what basis?
cases.ruling: The Court en banc denied the second motion for reconsideration but changed the basis of PSI's liability. (1) Not respondeat superior: under the control test, an employment relationship exists only if the hospital controls both the means and the details of how the doctor does his work. Both lower courts found that Dr. Ampil was a consultant, not an employee, the Aganas never questioned that finding, and there was not enough evidence of control. (2) Ostensible agency (apparent authority): PSI held Dr. Ampil out as its agent, and Natividad's husband chose him because he believed Dr. Ampil was a staff member of a prominent hospital; PSI's "consent for hospital care" form, referring to "the physicians of this hospital," reinforced that belief. (3) Corporate negligence: by its own admission PSI had the power and duty to review what happened within its walls; its duty to initiate a review of the reported missing gauzes was non-delegable, and it did nothing. This corporate negligence is distinct from Dr. Ampil's medical negligence and makes PSI directly liable. The liability based on ostensible agency and corporate negligence was declared pro hac vice (for this case only, not a precedent). PSI was ordered to pay ₱15 million with 12% interest a year from finality.
cases.keyDoctrine: A hospital may be liable for a doctor's negligence on three bases: (1) respondeat superior, where there is an employment relationship, determined by the control test (control of both the means and the details of the doctor's work); (2) apparent authority, where the hospital holds the doctor out as its agent and the patient relies on it; and (3) corporate negligence, a direct liability for the hospital's own failure as a corporation, distinct from the doctor's medical negligence. The Court applied the last two to PSI pro hac vice.

cases.name: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
cases.subject: Civil Law
cases.facts: Marissa Baco, 35, was in her fourth pregnancy; her obstetrician, Dr. Ma. Ditas F. Dela Cruz, had delivered her previous child by cesarean section. At 30 to 31 weeks she had bleeding and labor pains and was admitted to the Manila East Medical Center (MEMCI). Dr. Dela Cruz ordered tocolysis (medication to delay premature delivery) and monitoring, but no ultrasound or MRI was done during her confinement; the doctor relied on an ultrasound taken more than a month earlier. The next afternoon Marissa bled profusely again. During the emergency cesarean section the doctor found the placenta deeply attached to the uterine wall (placenta accreta) and removed the uterus, but blood for her rare type AB had not been secured in time, and Marissa died. Her premature baby, Julia Carla, died the next day. Her partner, children and parents sued the doctor and the hospital for damages. The trial court and the Court of Appeals dismissed the complaint, mainly because the family presented no expert witness (their medico-legal officer's testimony was stricken off when she did not appear for cross-examination).
cases.issue: (1) Does res ipsa loquitur apply? (2) Were the doctor and the hospital negligent, entitling the heirs to damages?
cases.ruling: The Court reversed and held the doctor and the hospital solidarily liable. (1) Res ipsa loquitur did not apply: it is applied only in exceptional cases where the lapse is readily apparent to a layman and within the physician's exclusive control. Placenta accreta is not immediately apparent and often not immediately diagnosed, and it arose from the pregnancy itself, not under the doctor's exclusive control, so expert testimony was needed. (2) The failure to present an expert does not always bar recovery: the defendant doctor's own expert can establish the standard of care and indirectly support the patient's claim. Here the defense expert admitted that ultrasound and MRI help diagnose placenta accreta; his statement that he would have acted the same way referred only to the emergency surgery. Given Marissa's high-risk history, Dr. Dela Cruz should have anticipated complications, ordered an ultrasound or MRI during the hours of relative calm, and secured blood in advance; timely diagnosis could have averted both deaths. MEMCI was vicariously liable even though Dr. Dela Cruz was only a consultant: under apparent authority a representation may be general and implied, and the hospital held her out as a member of its staff by letting her use its facilities and direct its nurses and specialists. The heirs were awarded actual, moral and exemplary damages, civil indemnity, attorney's fees and interest.
cases.keyDoctrine: Res ipsa loquitur applies in medical cases only in exceptional circumstances, where the lack of due care is readily apparent to a layman and within the physician's exclusive control; it does not apply where the actual cause of the injury has been identified. The plaintiff's lack of an expert witness is not fatal if the defense's own expert establishes the standard of care and indirectly supports the claim. Under apparent authority, a hospital's representation that a doctor is part of its staff may be general and implied, such as by letting the doctor use its facilities and direct its staff.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What is medical malpractice, and what must a patient prove to hold a physician liable for it? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Medical malpractice is a particular form of negligence: the failure of a physician or surgeon to apply to his practice that degree of care and skill ordinarily employed by the profession generally, under similar conditions and in like surrounding circumstances. The patient must prove four elements: duty, breach, injury and proximate causation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital: a patient must prove that the physician either failed to do something a reasonably prudent physician would have done, or did something a reasonably prudent physician would not have done, and that the failure or action caused injury to the patient. The duty arises from the physician-patient relationship; the physician must use at least the level of care a reasonably competent doctor would use under the same circumstances. Because the causes of injuries in malpractice cases are determinable only in the light of scientific knowledge, expert testimony is usually necessary to prove the standard of care, its breach and causation.
suggestedAnswer.application: A patient who sues must therefore show (1) a physician-patient relationship giving rise to the duty; (2) a departure from what a reasonably prudent physician would do; (3) an injury; and (4) that the departure, not something else, caused the injury, ordinarily through a qualified expert. The only exception the Court recognized is res ipsa loquitur, where the injury itself shows negligence.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Medical malpractice is negligence measured against the care and skill ordinarily employed by the profession, proved through duty, breach, injury and proximate causation, usually with expert testimony. **Bar trap:** a bad result alone is not malpractice; the patient must show a breach of the standard of care that caused the injury.

keyPoints: Definition: failure to apply the degree of care and skill ordinarily employed by the profession generally, under similar conditions
Four elements: duty, breach, injury, proximate causation
Duty comes from the physician-patient relationship
Expert testimony is usually needed to prove the standard of care, breach and causation (res ipsa loquitur is the exception)

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, the nature and elements of medical malpractice
source.excerpt: Petitioner’s action is for medical malpractice. This is a particular form of negligence which consists in the failure of a physician or surgeon to apply to his practice of medicine that degree of care and skill which is ordinarily employed by the profession generally, under similar conditions, and in like surrounding circumstances. In order to successfully pursue such a claim, a patient must prove that the physician or surgeon either failed to do something which a reasonably prudent physician or surgeon would have done, or that he or she did something that a reasonably prudent physician or surgeon would not have done, and that the failure or action caused injury to the patient. There are thus four elements involved in medical negligence cases, namely: duty, breach, injury, and proximate causation. … As to this aspect of medical malpractice, the determination of the reasonable level of care and the breach thereof, expert testimony is essential. Inasmuch as the causes of the injuries involved in malpractice actions are determinable only in the light of scientific knowledge, it has been recognized that expert testimony is usually necessary to support the conclusion as to causation.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Discuss the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur in medical negligence cases. What are its requisites, what is its effect, and when does it not apply?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Res ipsa loquitur ("the thing speaks for itself") lets the court find a physician negligent without expert testimony, because the injury itself provides the proof of negligence. It applies only where a layman can tell from common knowledge that the result would not have happened if due care had been used, and never to a suit on the merits of a diagnosis or a scientific treatment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital (quoting Ramos v. Court of Appeals), the requisites are: (1) the accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge; and (3) the injury was not due to any voluntary action or contribution of the person injured. When the doctrine applies, the patient need only prove a nexus between the act or omission complained of and the injury sustained while under the defendant's custody. It is not a rigid doctrine to be perfunctorily used, but a rule to be cautiously applied.
suggestedAnswer.application: It has been applied, for example, to a foreign object left in the body after an operation, an injury to a healthy part of the body not under treatment, removal of the wrong body part, and brain damage of a neurologically sound patient during a routine gallbladder operation (Ramos). It does not apply where the patient, already seriously ill, simply did not recover, or where the claim questions whether a diagnosis was correct or a treatment worked: the physician is not required at his peril to explain why a diagnosis was not correct or a treatment did not produce the desired result.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The doctrine dispenses with expert testimony only in cases within common knowledge. **Bar trap:** distinguish the failure to secure results (no presumption of negligence) from the occurrence of something unusual that does not ordinarily happen with proper care (res ipsa loquitur).

keyPoints: Meaning: the injury itself provides the proof of negligence; expert testimony is dispensed with
Requisites: an accident that does not ordinarily occur without negligence; exclusive control by the defendant; no voluntary action or contribution of the injured person
Applied to matters within common knowledge, e.g., a foreign object left in the body, the wrong body part removed
Does not apply to the merits of a diagnosis or of a scientific treatment; failure to secure results is not negligence

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Res Ipsa Loquitur
source.excerpt: There is a case when expert testimony may be dispensed with, and that is under the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur. … when the doctrine of res ipsa loquitor is availed by the plaintiff, the need for expert medical testimony is dispensed with because the injury itself provides the proof of negligence. … Thus, courts of other jurisdictions have applied the doctrine in the following situations: leaving of a foreign object in the body of the patient after an operation, injuries sustained on a healthy part of the body which was not under, or in the area, of treatment, removal of the wrong part of the body when another part was intended … Petitioners now contend that all requisites for the application of res ipsa loquitur were present, namely: (1) the accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge; and (3) the injury suffered must not have been due to any voluntary action or contribution of the person injured. … Res ipsa loquitur is not a rigid or ordinary doctrine to be perfunctorily used but a rule to be cautiously applied, depending upon the circumstances of each case. … A distinction must be made between the failure to secure results, and the occurrence of something more unusual and not ordinarily found if the service or treatment rendered followed the usual procedure of those skilled in that particular practice. It must be conceded that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur can have no application in a suit against a physician or a surgeon which involves the merits of a diagnosis or of a scientific treatment. The physician or surgeon is not required at his peril to explain why any particular diagnosis was not correct, or why any particular scientific treatment did not produce the desired result.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient's heirs sue her doctor for damages. Their lawyer argues that the practice of medicine, like the business of a common carrier, is affected with public interest, so doctors must observe extraordinary diligence toward their patients, and any lapse below that makes the doctor liable. Is the argument correct? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Doctors are not bound to observe extraordinary diligence; that standard is peculiar to common carriers. A doctor is bound to the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Article 1733 of the Civil Code imposes extraordinary diligence on common carriers, from the nature of their business and for reasons of public policy. In Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, the Court held that this standard is peculiar to common carriers. The practice of medicine is engaged in only by licensed, regulated professionals who are also bound by the Hippocratic Oath, so there is no need to require extraordinary diligence of them; the practice of medicine is already conditioned on the highest degree of diligence. The standard is not the average merit of all known practitioners, from the best to the worst, but the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians.
suggestedAnswer.application: That medicine, like common carriage, is affected with public interest does not import the carrier's standard into medical cases. The heirs must prove that the doctor fell below the care and skill of ordinarily good physicians under similar circumstances, which usually needs expert testimony, not merely that the doctor could have been more careful.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The argument is wrong. The doctor's duty is reasonable diligence: the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians. **Bar trap:** "affected with public interest" sounds like it leads to extraordinary diligence, but only common carriers are held to it.

keyPoints: Extraordinary diligence is peculiar to common carriers (Art. 1733, Civil Code)
Medicine is a licensed, state-regulated profession, also governed by the Hippocratic Oath
The standard for doctors is the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians, not the average of all practitioners
The heirs must still prove a breach of that standard, usually through expert testimony

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Fourth (the diligence required of doctors)
source.excerpt: Indeed, the standard contemplated is not what is actually the average merit among all known practitioners from the best to the worst and from the most to the least experienced, but the reasonable average merit among the ordinarily good physicians. … The standard of extraordinary diligence is peculiar to common carriers. … The practice of medicine is a profession engaged in only by qualified individuals. It is a right earned through years of education, training, and by first obtaining a license from the state through professional board examinations. Such license may, at any time and for cause, be revoked by the government. In addition to state regulation, the conduct of doctors is also strictly governed by the Hippocratic Oath, an ancient code of discipline and ethical rules which doctors have imposed upon themselves in recognition and acceptance of their great responsibility to society. Given these safeguards, there is no need to expressly require of doctors the observance of "extraordinary" diligence. As it is now, the practice of medicine is already conditioned upon the highest degree of diligence. And, as we have already noted, the standard contemplated for doctors is simply the reasonable average merit among ordinarily good physicians.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The failure of a physician or surgeon to apply to his practice of medicine that degree of care and skill which is ordinarily employed by the profession generally, under similar conditions and in like surrounding circumstances, is known as

choices.A: medical malpractice.
choices.B: res ipsa loquitur.
choices.C: corporate negligence.
choices.D: the captain of the ship doctrine.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** In Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, the Court defined medical malpractice as "a particular form of negligence" consisting in that failure. **B is wrong:** res ipsa loquitur is a rule of evidence that lets negligence be inferred from the injury itself; it is not the wrong. **C is wrong:** corporate negligence is the hospital's own failure in its duties as an institution, not a physician's lack of care and skill. **D is wrong:** the captain of the ship doctrine places the operating surgeon in complete charge of the operating room; it decides who is responsible, not what malpractice is. **Bar trap:** these doctrine names often appear together as choices; tie each to what it does.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Pedro had a high fever and chills for six days that his own medicines did not relieve. He was admitted to a clinic, diagnosed with typhoid fever through a standard test, and given the drug of choice. He died nine hours later. His heirs sue the doctors and invoke res ipsa loquitur so they need not present an expert. Will the doctrine apply?

choices.A: Yes, because a patient who walked into the clinic conscious and coherent would not ordinarily die within hours unless someone was negligent.
choices.B: Yes, because Pedro was under the exclusive control of the clinic and its doctors when he died.
choices.C: No, because his death after a serious illness was not unusual, and the claim questions the merits of a diagnosis and treatment, which needs expert opinion.
choices.D: No, because res ipsa loquitur never applies to suits against physicians and surgeons.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** In Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, the patient had fever and chills for five days before admission and died about ten hours after. The Court held there was nothing unusual or extraordinary about his death, since he was already seriously ill and help came too late; the alleged lapse was not apparent to a layman; and res ipsa loquitur has no application to a suit that involves the merits of a diagnosis or of a scientific treatment. **A is wrong:** the speed of death alone does not show negligence when the patient was already gravely ill; that was the very argument the Court rejected. **B is wrong:** exclusive control is only one requisite; the first (an injury that does not ordinarily occur without negligence) was missing. **D is wrong:** the doctrine does apply in proper malpractice cases, for example a foreign object left in the body, or brain damage during a routine anesthesia as in Ramos. **Bar trap:** a sudden death in the hospital tempts you to say "the thing speaks for itself"; ask first whether a layman could tell that it would not have happened with due care.

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Res Ipsa Loquitur (application to the facts)
source.excerpt: In this case, while it is true that the patient died just a few hours after professional medical assistance was rendered, there is really nothing unusual or extraordinary about his death. Prior to his admission, the patient already had recurring fevers and chills for five days unrelieved by the analgesic, antipyretic, and antibiotics given him by his wife. This shows that he had been suffering from a serious illness and professional medical help came too late for him. Respondents alleged failure to observe due care was not immediately apparent to a layman so as to justify application of res ipsa loquitur. The question required expert opinion on the alleged breach by respondents of the standard of care required by the circumstances.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: As enumerated in Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, which of the following is NOT a requisite for the application of res ipsa loquitur?

choices.A: The accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent.
choices.B: The instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge.
choices.C: The injury suffered was not due to any voluntary action or contribution of the person injured.
choices.D: The defendant physician admitted a departure from the standard medical procedure.

questions.explanation: **D is correct (it is not a requisite).** The requisites listed in Reyes are A, B and C: an accident that does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent, exclusive control of what caused the injury by the person in charge, and no voluntary action or contribution of the injured person. An admission by the doctor is not needed; the whole point of the doctrine is that the injury itself provides the proof of negligence, without expert or direct proof. **A, B and C are wrong answers** because each is one of the three requisites. **Bar trap:** a requisite that sounds like extra proof (an admission, an expert's opinion) is the opposite of what res ipsa loquitur is for.

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Res Ipsa Loquitur (the requisites)
source.excerpt: Petitioners now contend that all requisites for the application of res ipsa loquitur were present, namely: (1) the accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge; and (3) the injury suffered must not have been due to any voluntary action or contribution of the person injured.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a suit claiming that doctors misdiagnosed typhoid fever and gave a fatal drug, the heirs' only expert is a pathologist who performed the autopsy. He is not a specialist in infectious diseases, has never autopsied a typhoid victim, and has seen only about three typhoid cases. Following Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, how should his opinion that the doctors erred in their diagnosis be treated?

choices.A: It must be given full weight, because a pathologist who performed the autopsy is always the best witness on the cause of death.
choices.B: It was properly discarded, because he was not qualified to prove that the doctor erred in diagnosing typhoid fever.
choices.C: It shifts the burden to the doctors to prove that the patient died of typhoid fever.
choices.D: It is unnecessary, because the heirs may rely on res ipsa loquitur to prove a wrong diagnosis.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held that the pathologist was not an expert on the matter: he was not a specialist on infectious diseases like typhoid fever, had not yet autopsied a typhoid victim, and had treated only about three typhoid cases; so he was "not qualified to prove that Dr. Marlyn Rico erred in her diagnosis," and the lower courts correctly discarded his testimony. **A is wrong:** the expert must be qualified on the very question in issue (here, the diagnosis of an infectious disease), not merely have examined the body. **C is wrong:** the burden of proving that the patient had another illness stayed with the heirs, who failed to present expert opinion on it. **D is wrong:** res ipsa loquitur has no application to the merits of a diagnosis. **Bar trap:** compare Ramos, where a pulmonologist's opinion on anesthesia was rejected for the same reason; the expert's field must match the issue.

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Specific Acts of Negligence (First: the qualification of the expert)
source.excerpt: First. While petitioners presented Dr. Apolinar Vacalares as an expert witness, we do not find him to be so as he is not a specialist on infectious diseases like typhoid fever. Furthermore, although he may have had extensive experience in performing autopsies, he admitted that he had yet to do one on the body of a typhoid victim at the time he conducted the postmortem on Jorge Reyes. It is also plain from his testimony that he has treated only about three cases of typhoid fever. … He is thus not qualified to prove that Dr. Marlyn Rico erred in her diagnosis. Both lower courts were therefore correct in discarding his testimony, which is really inadmissible.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient dies of a rare allergic reaction to an antibiotic, despite a negative skin test done before the drug was given. Under the ruling in Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, does the reaction alone establish the doctors' negligence?

choices.A: Yes, because doctors must guarantee that no drug they prescribe will cause a harmful reaction.
choices.B: Yes, because a negative skin test that turns out wrong is proof that the test was performed negligently.
choices.C: No, but only because the patient's family consented to the treatment.
choices.D: No, because the law requires doctors only to perform the standard tests and procedures; it cannot require them to predict every possible reaction to every drug.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** Quoting the Court of Appeals with approval, the Court held that even if the patient suffered an anaphylactic shock, "this, of itself, would not yet establish the negligence of the appellee-physicians for all that the law requires of them is that they perform the standard tests and perform standard procedures. The law cannot require them to predict every possible reaction to all drugs administered." The burden was on the heirs to show that the doctors ignored standard procedure. **A is wrong:** doctors are not guarantors of results. **B is wrong:** the Court noted that skin testing with such drugs is generally not reliable, so a negative test does not rule out a reaction. **C is wrong:** consent was not the basis of the ruling; the doctors were not negligent because they followed standard procedure. **Bar trap:** an adverse outcome is not, by itself, a breach of the standard of care.

source.caseTitle: Reyes, et al. v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital, et al.
source.part: Ruling, Third (the standard tests and procedures)
source.excerpt: What all this means legally is that even if the deceased suffered from an anaphylactic shock, this, of itself, would not yet establish the negligence of the appellee-physicians for all that the law requires of them is that they perform the standard tests and perform standard procedures. The law cannot require them to predict every possible reaction to all drugs administered. The onus probandi was on the appellants to establish, before the trial court, that the appellee-physicians ignored standard medical procedure, prescribed and administered medication with recklessness and exhibited an absence of the competence and skills expected of general practitioners similarly situated.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Two general-surgery residents examined a girl in the emergency room after a motorcycle ran over her foot. They had only the foot X-rayed, found no fracture, refused the mother's request for an X-ray of the whole leg, and assured her that her daughter was fine. Two weeks later a fracture of the shinbone was found. Charged with reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries, the residents were acquitted because the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the delay aggravated the injury. The mother now asks whether the residents can still be made to pay damages, and the residents answer that the motorcycle rider, not they, caused the fracture. Decide.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The residents may be held civilly liable despite their acquittal, and they cannot shift the liability to the motorcycle rider.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Jarcia v. People, the Court acquitted two emergency-room residents of reckless imprudence because their guilt was not proved beyond reasonable doubt, but held them civilly liable, since a criminal conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt while civil liability needs only a preponderance of evidence. It also held that doctors cannot invoke the fact that the accident was the actual, direct and proximate cause of the injury to excuse themselves; otherwise doctors would have a ready defense whenever they fail to do their job for victims of accidents and crimes of violence.
suggestedAnswer.application: The residents were negligent: they did not examine the leg thoroughly, refused the X-ray the mother asked for, and assured her that all was well instead of referring the child to a doctor who could properly examine her. That suffices for civil liability on a preponderance of evidence, even if it did not reach proof beyond reasonable doubt. The rider caused the fracture, but the residents' own failure to attend to the child's injuries is a separate fault for which they answer.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The residents are civilly liable for damages even though acquitted. **Bar trap:** do not reason that an acquittal ends all liability, or that the person who caused the original injury is the only one liable.

keyPoints: Acquittal for lack of proof beyond reasonable doubt does not bar civil liability, which needs only a preponderance of evidence
The residents were negligent: no thorough examination, no referral, a baseless assurance that all was well
Doctors cannot escape liability by pointing to the accident as the direct and proximate cause of the injury
Otherwise doctors would have a ready defense whenever they fail to properly attend to accident or crime victims

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to Dr. Jarcia and Dr. Bastan's negligence; As to the Award of Damages
source.excerpt: There was, however, no precise evidence and scientific explanation pointing to the fact that the delay in the application of the cast to the patient’s fractured leg because of failure to immediately diagnose the specific injury of the patient, prolonged the pain of the child or aggravated his condition or even caused further complications. … The Court, nevertheless, finds the petitioners civilly liable for their failure to sufficiently attend to Roy Jr.’s medical needs when the latter was rushed to the ER, for while a criminal conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, only a preponderance of evidence is required to establish civil liability. Taken into account also was the fact that there was no bad faith on their part. Dr. Jarcia and Dr. Bastan cannot pass on the liability to the taxi driver who hit the victim. It may be true that the actual, direct, immediate, and proximate cause of the injury (fracture of the leg bone or tibia) of Roy Jr. was the vehicular accident when he was hit by a taxi. The petitioners, however, cannot simply invoke such fact alone to excuse themselves from any liability. If this would be so, doctors would have a ready defense should they fail to do their job in attending to victims of hit-and-run, maltreatment, and other crimes of violence in which the actual, direct, immediate, and proximate cause of the injury is indubitably the act of the perpetrator/s.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Is res ipsa loquitur a rule of substantive law? Explain its nature and when it may be invoked, and state whether it applies against emergency-room residents who failed to detect a fracture in a boy injured in a vehicular accident.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Res ipsa loquitur is not a rule of substantive law but merely a mode of proof, a procedural convenience. It may be invoked only when direct evidence is absent and not readily available. It did not apply to the emergency-room residents.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Jarcia v. People, the Court explained that the doctrine, as a rule of evidence, recognizes that prima facie negligence may be established without direct proof and furnishes a substitute for specific proof of negligence. It does not dispense with proof of culpable negligence; it only determines what shall be prima facie evidence of it and helps the plaintiff prove a breach of duty. Its requisites are: (1) the accident does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality that caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge; and (3) the injury was not due to any voluntary action or contribution of the injured person.
suggestedAnswer.application: The circumstances that caused the boy's injury, and the tests needed to find its extent, were not under the exclusive control of the residents, who merely attended to him in the emergency room. Whether they used the required skill and care was a matter for expert opinion, not for the assumptions of a layman like the boy's mother. So the Court of Appeals erred in applying the doctrine.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Res ipsa loquitur is an evidentiary rule, not a ground of liability, and it did not apply. **Bar trap:** even a clearly negligent doctor (the residents here were found civilly negligent) may not be reached through res ipsa loquitur when exclusive control is missing; the two questions are separate.

keyPoints: Not a rule of substantive law; a mode of proof or procedural convenience
It does not dispense with proof of negligence; it only makes out a prima facie case
Invoked only when direct evidence is absent and not readily available
Requisites: accident not ordinarily occurring without negligence; exclusive control; no contribution by the injured
Not applicable here: no exclusive control by the residents; the skill and care issue needed expert opinion

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to the Application of The Doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur
source.excerpt: The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur as a rule of evidence is unusual to the law of negligence which recognizes that prima facie negligence may be established without direct proof and furnishes a substitute for specific proof of negligence. The doctrine, however, is not a rule of substantive law, but merely a mode of proof or a mere procedural convenience. The rule, when applicable to the facts and circumstances of a given case, is not meant to and does not dispense with the requirement of proof of culpable negligence on the party charged. It merely determines and regulates what shall be prima facie evidence thereof and helps the plaintiff in proving a breach of the duty. The doctrine can be invoked when and only when, under the circumstances involved, direct evidence is absent and not readily available. The requisites for the application of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur are: (1) the accident was of a kind which does not ordinarily occur unless someone is negligent; (2) the instrumentality or agency which caused the injury was under the exclusive control of the person in charge; and (3) the injury suffered must not have been due to any voluntary action or contribution of the person injured. In this case, the circumstances that caused patient Roy Jr.’s injury and the series of tests that were supposed to be undergone by him to determine the extent of the injury suffered were not under the exclusive control of Drs. Jarcia and Bastan. … As to whether the petitioners have exercised the requisite degree of skill and care in treating patient Roy, Jr. is generally a matter of expert opinion.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Sued for damages, two doctors argue for the first time before the Supreme Court that no physician-patient relationship existed, because they were not the boy's attending physicians and had merely been asked by a nurse to look at him while they were passing by the emergency room on their way to lunch. They had examined him and told his mother that he was fine and could go home. Will the argument prosper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The issue cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, and in any case a physician-patient relationship arose when the doctors examined the boy and assured his mother.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Jarcia v. People, the Court held that issues raised for the first time on appeal cannot be considered, because a party may not change his theory on appeal. Quoting Lucas v. Tuaño, it held that when a patient engages the services of a physician, a physician-patient relationship is generated; by accepting a case the physician represents that he has the needed training and skill of physicians practicing in the same field and will employ them, and he must exercise the care, skill and diligence that physicians in the same general neighborhood and the same general line of practice ordinarily possess and exercise in like cases.
suggestedAnswer.application: The boy and his mother went to the emergency room for immediate medical attention. The doctors obliged: they examined him and assured the mother that everything was fine and that they could go home. Having taken him on, they owed him the standard of care; if they were not in a position to attend to him properly, they should have referred him to a doctor who could, instead of giving a baseless assurance.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense fails, both procedurally and on the merits. **Bar trap:** "I was only passing by" is no defense once the doctor examines the patient and gives assurances.

keyPoints: A new theory cannot be raised for the first time on appeal
A physician-patient relationship arises when the physician accepts the case (here, by examining the boy and assuring the mother)
By accepting a case the physician represents he has and will use the skill of physicians in the same field
Standard: care, skill and diligence of physicians in the same general neighborhood and line of practice
If unable to attend properly, the doctor should refer the patient instead of giving baseless assurances

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, on the physician-patient relationship
source.excerpt: Firstly, this issue was never raised during the trial at the RTC or even before the CA. The petitioners, therefore, raise the want of doctor-patient relationship for the first time on appeal with this Court. It has been settled that "issues raised for the first time on appeal cannot be considered because a party is not permitted to change his theory on appeal. … In the case of Lucas v. Tuaño, the Court wrote that "[w]hen a patient engages the services of a physician, a physician-patient relationship is generated. And in accepting a case, the physician, for all intents and purposes, represents that he has the needed training and skill possessed by physicians and surgeons practicing in the same field; and that he will employ such training, care, and skill in the treatment of the patient. Thus, in treating his patient, a physician is under a duty to exercise that degree of care, skill and diligence which physicians in the same general neighborhood and in the same general line of practice ordinarily possess and exercise in like cases. … Indubitably, a physician-patient relationship exists between the petitioners and patient Roy Jr. Notably, the latter and his mother went to the ER for an immediate medical attention. The petitioners allegedly passed by and were requested to attend to the victim (contrary to the testimony of Dr. Tacata that they were, at that time, residents on duty at the ER). They obliged and examined the victim, and later assured the mother that everything was fine and that they could go home. Clearly, a physician-patient relationship was established between the petitioners and the patient Roy Jr.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Jarcia v. People, the Court of Appeals relied on res ipsa loquitur to uphold the conviction of two emergency-room residents who failed to detect a boy's leg fracture. How did the Supreme Court rule on the use of the doctrine?

choices.A: It was correctly applied, because the residents had exclusive control over which X-rays would be requested.
choices.B: It was wrongly applied, because the circumstances that caused the injury and the tests to determine its extent were not under the residents' exclusive control, and their skill and care were a matter for expert opinion.
choices.C: It was correctly applied, because the mother, being a nurse, could testify on the standard of care without an expert.
choices.D: It was wrongly applied, because res ipsa loquitur is never allowed in a criminal case.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held that the circumstances that caused the boy's injury and the tests he was supposed to undergo were not under the exclusive control of the residents, who merely attended to him at the emergency room, and that whether they used the required skill and care was best shown by expert witnesses, not the assumptions of a layman like the mother. **A is wrong:** that was the Court of Appeals' reasoning, which the Supreme Court rejected. **C is wrong:** the Court treated the mother as a layman; her opinion could not replace expert testimony. **D is wrong:** the Court did not rest its ruling on the case being criminal; it found the requisites missing on the facts. **Bar trap:** exclusive control is the requisite most often missing for a doctor who treats an injury caused elsewhere.

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to the Application of The Doctrine of Res Ipsa Loquitur
source.excerpt: In this case, the circumstances that caused patient Roy Jr.’s injury and the series of tests that were supposed to be undergone by him to determine the extent of the injury suffered were not under the exclusive control of Drs. Jarcia and Bastan. It was established that they are mere residents of the Manila Doctors Hospital at that time who attended to the victim at the emergency room. While it may be true that the circumstances pointed out by the courts below seem doubtless to constitute reckless imprudence on the part of the petitioners, this conclusion is still best achieved, not through the scholarly assumptions of a layman like the patient’s mother, but by the unquestionable knowledge of expert witness/es. As to whether the petitioners have exercised the requisite degree of skill and care in treating patient Roy, Jr. is generally a matter of expert opinion.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: "The failure to observe for the protection of the interests of another person that degree of care, precaution, and vigilance which the circumstances justly demand, whereby such other person suffers injury." This is the definition of

choices.A: reckless imprudence.
choices.B: simple imprudence.
choices.C: negligence.
choices.D: malice.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** Jarcia v. People gives this as the definition of negligence. **A is wrong:** reckless imprudence is the quasi-offense of voluntarily doing or failing to do, without malice, an act from which material damage results by reason of an inexcusable lack of precaution; it requires more than the general definition. **B is wrong:** simple imprudence (simple negligence) has its own two elements, a lack of precaution and damage that is not immediate or a danger that is not clearly manifest. **D is wrong:** the Court's definitions describe negligence and imprudence as acts done without malice. **Bar trap:** negligence, simple imprudence and reckless imprudence are defined differently; match the definition to the term.

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to Dr. Jarcia and Dr. Bastan's negligence
source.excerpt: Negligence is defined as the failure to observe for the protection of the interests of another person that degree of care, precaution, and vigilance which the circumstances justly demand, whereby such other person suffers injury. Reckless imprudence consists of voluntarily doing or failing to do, without malice, an act from which material damage results by reason of an inexcusable lack of precaution on the part of the person performing or failing to perform such act.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Jarcia v. People, which of the following are the elements of simple negligence (simple imprudence)?

choices.A: (1) Lack of precaution on the part of the offender, and (2) the damage impending to be caused is not immediate or the danger is not clearly manifest.
choices.B: (1) An act done with malice, and (2) material damage resulting from it.
choices.C: (1) Inexcusable lack of precaution, and (2) immediate and clearly manifest danger.
choices.D: (1) A pre-existing contract, and (2) a breach of it causing damage.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court stated that the elements of simple negligence are: (1) lack of precaution on the part of the offender, and (2) the damage impending to be caused is not immediate or the danger is not clearly manifest. **B is wrong:** malice excludes negligence of any kind. **C is wrong:** an inexcusable lack of precaution describes reckless imprudence, and a clearly manifest danger is exactly what simple negligence lacks. **D is wrong:** that describes a breach of contract (culpa contractual), not simple negligence. **Bar trap:** simple and reckless imprudence differ in how immediate and manifest the danger is; the Court found neither proved beyond reasonable doubt in Jarcia.

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to Dr. Jarcia and Dr. Bastan's negligence (simple negligence)
source.excerpt: Reckless imprudence consists of voluntarily doing or failing to do, without malice, an act from which material damage results by reason of an inexcusable lack of precaution on the part of the person performing or failing to perform such act. The elements of simple negligence are: (1) that there is lack of precaution on the part of the offender, and (2) that the damage impending to be caused is not immediate or the danger is not clearly manifest.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Following Lucas v. Tuaño, as quoted in Jarcia v. People, what degree of care, skill and diligence must a physician exercise in treating a patient?

choices.A: The extraordinary diligence required of common carriers.
choices.B: The highest skill possessed by the best specialists anywhere in the world.
choices.C: Whatever care the patient expected when he engaged the physician.
choices.D: That which physicians in the same general neighborhood and in the same general line of practice ordinarily possess and exercise in like cases.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** Quoting Lucas v. Tuaño, the Court held that a physician "is under a duty to exercise that degree of care, skill and diligence which physicians in the same general neighborhood and in the same general line of practice ordinarily possess and exercise in like cases," that is, at least the level of care any other reasonably competent physician would use under similar circumstances. **A is wrong:** extraordinary diligence is peculiar to common carriers (Reyes v. Sisters of Mercy Hospital). **B is wrong:** the standard is ordinary competence in the same field, not the best in the world. **C is wrong:** the standard is objective, set by the profession, not by the patient's expectations. **Bar trap:** the comparison group is physicians in the same general line of practice, so a general surgeon is measured against general surgeons, not orthopedic specialists.

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, on the physician-patient relationship (quoting Lucas v. Tuaño)
source.excerpt: Thus, in treating his patient, a physician is under a duty to exercise that degree of care, skill and diligence which physicians in the same general neighborhood and in the same general line of practice ordinarily possess and exercise in like cases. Stated otherwise, the physician has the obligation to use at least the same level of care that any other reasonably competent physician would use to treat the condition under similar circumstances.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Jarcia v. People, after acquitting the two doctors of the crime charged, what did the Court do about damages?

choices.A: It deleted all damages, since there can be no civil liability without a criminal conviction.
choices.B: It held them civilly liable for actual, moral and exemplary damages, since civil liability needs only a preponderance of evidence.
choices.C: It held only the taxi driver liable for damages, since the accident was the proximate cause of the fracture.
choices.D: It awarded only actual damages, since moral damages are punitive and cannot be imposed on doctors acquitted of a crime.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held the doctors civilly liable for ₱3,850 actual damages, ₱100,000 moral damages and ₱50,000 exemplary damages, because "while a criminal conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, only a preponderance of evidence is required to establish civil liability." **A is wrong:** acquittal on reasonable doubt does not bar civil liability. **C is wrong:** the doctors could not pass on the liability to the taxi driver; their negligence was contributory. **D is wrong:** the Court said moral damages are not punitive but compensatory, and it awarded them together with exemplary damages. **Bar trap:** do not confuse the quantum of proof for the crime with that for civil liability.

source.caseTitle: Jarcia, Jr., et al. v. People
source.part: The Court's Ruling, As to the Award of Damages
source.excerpt: Although the Court sympathizes with the plight of the mother and the child in this case, the Court is bound by the dictates of justice which hold inviolable the right of the accused to be presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt. The Court, nevertheless, finds the petitioners civilly liable for their failure to sufficiently attend to Roy Jr.’s medical needs when the latter was rushed to the ER, for while a criminal conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, only a preponderance of evidence is required to establish civil liability. … While no criminal negligence was found in the petitioners’ failure to administer the necessary medical attention to Roy Jr., the Court holds them civilly liable for the resulting damages to their patient. While it was the taxi driver who ran over the foot or leg of Roy Jr., their negligence was doubtless contributory. … It is settled that moral damages are not punitive in nature, but are designed to compensate and alleviate in some way the physical suffering, mental anguish, fright, serious anxiety, besmirched reputation, wounded feelings, moral shock, social humiliation, and similar injury unjustly inflicted on a person.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur? State its requisites, and identify which of them is the most instrumental.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Res ipsa loquitur literally means "the thing speaks for itself." It is the rule that the fact of the occurrence of an injury, taken with the surrounding circumstances, may permit an inference or raise a presumption of negligence, or make out the plaintiff's prima facie case, and present a question of fact for the defendant to meet with an explanation.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cruz v. Agas, the Court listed its requisites: (1) the occurrence of an injury; (2) the thing which caused the injury was under the control and management of the defendant; (3) the occurrence was such that in the ordinary course of things it would not have happened if those who had control or management used proper care; and (4) the absence of explanation by the defendant. Of these, the most instrumental is the control and management of the thing which caused the injury.
suggestedAnswer.application: Applied to a doctor, the patient must show not only an injury but that what caused it was under the doctor's control and management, that it would not ordinarily happen with proper care, and that the doctor has no explanation. In Cruz, the doctor explained that the bleeding came from an abnormal condition of the patient's colon beyond his control, so the doctrine did not apply.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Res ipsa loquitur raises a presumption of negligence from the injury and its circumstances; control and management is its key requisite. **Bar trap:** the requisites are sometimes listed as three (e.g., Reyes, Jarcia) and sometimes as four (Cruz, adding the absence of explanation); either way, a satisfactory explanation by the defendant defeats the inference.

keyPoints: Literally "the thing speaks for itself"
The injury and its circumstances may raise a presumption of negligence or make out a prima facie case, which the defendant must meet with an explanation
Requisites: injury; control and management by the defendant; would not ordinarily happen with proper care; absence of explanation by the defendant
The most instrumental requisite is control and management of the thing that caused the injury

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Res Ipsa Loquitur Doctrine Not Applicable Against Respondent
source.excerpt: Literally, res ipsa loquitur means the thing speaks for itself. It is the rule that the fact of the occurrence of an injury, taken with the surrounding circumstances, may permit an inference or raise a presumption of negligence, or make out a plaintiff’s prima facie case, and present a question of fact for defendant to meet with an explanation. The requisites for the applicability of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur are: (1) the occurrence of an injury; (2) the thing which caused the injury was under the control and management of the defendant; (3) the occurrence was such that in the ordinary course of things, would not have happened if those who had control or management used proper care; and (4) the absence of explanation by the defendant. Of the foregoing requisites, the most instrumental is the control and management of the thing which caused the injury.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Rafael, a physician himself, underwent an endoscopic procedure and afterwards suffered internal bleeding that required surgery. In his complaint for reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries against the endoscopist, he narrated his symptoms and the surgery, stated that he was in good health before the procedure, and concluded that "something obviously went wrong." The prosecutor dismissed the complaint for lack of probable cause. Was the dismissal proper? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Rafael proved that he was injured, but not the specific negligent act or omission of the endoscopist that caused the injury, so negligence (an inexcusable lack of precaution) was not shown.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Cruz v. Agas, the Court held that a medical negligence case prospers only if the patient proves that the doctor failed to do something a reasonably prudent doctor would have done, or did something a reasonably prudent doctor would not have done, and that this caused the injury: duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. The patient has the burden of showing the particular negligent or reckless act or omission. Courts also do not interfere with the executive determination of probable cause in the absence of grave abuse of discretion.
suggestedAnswer.application: Rafael's complaint shows an injury and its consequences, but not what the endoscopist did or failed to do that a reasonably prudent specialist would not have done. "Something went wrong" is a conclusion, not proof of breach or causation. Without it there is no showing of inexcusable lack of precaution, and no grave abuse of discretion in finding no probable cause.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The dismissal was proper. **Bar trap:** an injury after treatment, and good health before it, do not by themselves prove negligence; the patient must point to the specific act or omission and its causal link to the injury.

keyPoints: Elements: duty, breach, injury and proximate causation
The patient has the burden of showing the specific negligent act or omission and that it caused the injury
An injury after a procedure, by itself, does not show inexcusable lack of precaution
Courts do not disturb the prosecutor's finding of no probable cause absent grave abuse of discretion

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Medical Negligence and Malpractice Not Established
source.excerpt: The settled policy is that the courts will not interfere with the executive determination of probable cause for the purpose of filing an Information, in the absence of grave abuse of discretion. … A medical negligence case can prosper if the patient can present solid proof that the doctor, like in this case, either failed to do something which a reasonably prudent doctor would have done, or that he did something that a reasonably prudent doctor would not have done, and such failure or action caused injury to the patient. … Simply put, the elements are duty, breach, injury and proximate causation. In this case, Dr. Cruz has the burden of showing the negligence or recklessness of Dr. Agas. Although there is no dispute that Dr. Cruz sustained internal hemorrhage due to a tear in the serosa of his sigmoid colon, he failed to show that it was caused by Dr. Agas’s negligent and reckless conduct of the colonoscopy procedure. In other words, Dr. Cruz failed to show and explain that particular negligent or reckless act or omission committed by Dr. Agas. Stated differently, Dr. Cruz did not demonstrate that there was "inexcusable lack of precaution" on the part of Dr. Agas.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Right after a colonoscopy, Ben suffered internal bleeding from a tear in the outermost layer of his colon and had part of his colon removed. The doctor showed that the tear came from adhesions and an abnormal twist of Ben's colon that no test could detect beforehand, and that the colonoscope passes only through the inside of the colon and could not reach the outermost layer. Ben argues that res ipsa loquitur applies, since he was healthy before the procedure and bled right after it. Is Ben correct? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The alleged negligence was not apparent to a layman, and the doctor explained the injury by a condition beyond his control, so res ipsa loquitur does not apply and expert opinion is needed to link the injury to the procedure.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Res ipsa loquitur requires, among others, that the thing which caused the injury was under the defendant's control and management, that the occurrence would not ordinarily happen with proper care, and the absence of explanation by the defendant (Cruz v. Agas). In Cruz, the Court held that the doctor's purported negligence was not immediately apparent to a layman, and that the bleeding was due to the abnormal condition and configuration of the patient's colon, beyond the doctor's control and undetectable before the procedure.
suggestedAnswer.application: Ben's bleeding came from the outermost layer of the colon, which the colonoscope inside the colon could not reach without a perforation, and from adhesions no test could have revealed. The cause was thus explained and was not within the doctor's control; whether the procedure caused the tear is a question for medical experts, not common knowledge.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Ben cannot rely on res ipsa loquitur; he must prove negligence through expert testimony. **Bar trap:** timing is not proof; the doctrine yields when the defendant explains the injury by a cause outside his control.

keyPoints: The negligence was not immediately apparent to a layman
The injury came from the patient's abnormal condition, beyond the doctor's control and undetectable beforehand
The doctor gave an explanation, defeating a requisite of the doctrine
Linking the injury to the procedure required expert opinion

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Res Ipsa Loquitur Doctrine Not Applicable Against Respondent (application)
source.excerpt: In this case, the Court agrees with Dr. Agas that his purported negligence in performing the colonoscopy on Dr. Cruz was not immediately apparent to a layman to justify the application of res ipsa loquitur doctrine. Dr. Agas was able to establish that the internal bleeding sustained by Dr. Cruz was due to the abnormal condition and configuration of his sigmoid colon which was beyond his control considering that the said condition could not be detected before a colonoscopic procedure. … On the other hand, in the present case, the correlation between petitioner’s injury, i.e., tear in the serosa of sigmoid colon, and the colonoscopy conducted by respondent to the petitioner clearly requires the presentation of an expert opinion considering that no perforation of the sigmoid colon was ever noted during the laparotomy. It cannot be overemphasized that the colonoscope inserted by the respondent only passed through the inside of petitioner’s sigmoid colon while the damaged tissue, i.e., serosa, which caused the bleeding, is located in the outermost layer of the colon.

choices.A: proximate cause.
choices.B: respondeat superior.

Agas: "Literally, res ipsa loquitur means the thing speaks for itself," and it is the rule described in the question. **A is wrong:** proximate cause is the cause that, in natural and continuous sequence, produces the injury; it is an element of negligence, not a rule of inference. **B is wrong:** respondeat superior makes an employer answer for an employee's negligence. **C is wrong:** corporate negligence is a hospital's own failure in its duties as an institution. **Bar trap:** identification items list several real doctrines as choices; tie each to its function.
