questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Cruz v. Agas, which of the requisites of res ipsa loquitur is the most instrumental?

choices.A: The control and management of the thing which caused the injury.
choices.B: The occurrence of an injury.
choices.C: The absence of explanation by the defendant.
choices.D: The presentation of an expert witness by the plaintiff.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** After listing the four requisites, the Court said: "Of the foregoing requisites, the most instrumental is the control and management of the thing which caused the injury." **B and C are wrong:** they are requisites too, but not the one the Court singled out. **D is wrong:** it is not a requisite at all; the doctrine exists precisely to dispense with expert proof where the injury speaks for itself. **Bar trap:** in PSI v. Agana the Court absolved the second surgeon for the same reason: the gauzes were under the lead surgeon's control and management, not his.

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Res Ipsa Loquitur Doctrine Not Applicable Against Respondent (the requisites)
source.excerpt: The requisites for the applicability of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur are: (1) the occurrence of an injury; (2) the thing which caused the injury was under the control and management of the defendant; (3) the occurrence was such that in the ordinary course of things, would not have happened if those who had control or management used proper care; and (4) the absence of explanation by the defendant. Of the foregoing requisites, the most instrumental is the control and management of the thing which caused the injury.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a medical negligence case, the patient must prove which of the following elements?

choices.A: Consent, injury, causation and malice.
choices.B: Duty, breach, injury and proximate causation.
choices.C: Contract, breach, damage and bad faith.
choices.D: Duty, injury, an expert's certification and exclusive control.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** Cruz v. Agas: a patient must prove that the health care provider failed to do what a reasonably prudent provider would have done, or did what a reasonably prudent provider would not have done, and that this caused injury; "[s]imply put, the elements are duty, breach, injury and proximate causation." **A is wrong:** malice is not an element of negligence, and consent is a separate issue (informed consent). **C is wrong:** that describes a breach of contract; bad faith is not required. **D is wrong:** exclusive control is a requisite of res ipsa loquitur, not an element of medical negligence, and there is no "expert's certification" element. **Bar trap:** do not mix the elements of medical negligence with the requisites of res ipsa loquitur.

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Medical Negligence and Malpractice Not Established (the elements)
source.excerpt: To successfully pursue this kind of case, a patient must only prove that a health care provider either failed to do something which a reasonably prudent health care provider would have done, or that he did something that a reasonably prudent provider would not have done; and that failure or action caused injury to the patient. Simply put, the elements are duty, breach, injury and proximate causation.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A patient's criminal complaint for reckless imprudence against his doctor is dismissed by the prosecutor for lack of probable cause, and the Secretary of Justice affirms. Following Cruz v. Agas, when will the courts set aside that finding?

choices.A: Whenever the court, weighing the evidence anew, would have found probable cause.
choices.B: Whenever the complainant is himself a physician who can explain the medical issues.
choices.C: Only when the finding is tainted with grave abuse of discretion, so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or a virtual refusal to perform a duty enjoined by law.
choices.D: Never, because the determination of probable cause is not subject to judicial review.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court held that under the doctrine of separation of powers, courts will not interfere with the executive determination of probable cause in the absence of grave abuse of discretion, which "must be so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or a virtual refusal to perform a duty enjoined by law." **A is wrong:** courts may not substitute their own judgment for the Executive's. **B is wrong:** the complainant's profession does not change the standard (Dr. Cruz was himself a physician and still lost). **D is wrong:** review is possible, but only for grave abuse of discretion. **Bar trap:** "never reviewable" and "freely reviewable" are both wrong; the test is grave abuse of discretion.

source.caseTitle: Cruz v. Agas, Jr.
source.part: Non-interference with Executive Determination of Probable Cause in Preliminary Investigations
source.excerpt: Under the doctrine of separation of powers, courts have no right to directly decide on matters over which full discretionary authority has been delegated to the Executive Branch of the Government, or to substitute their own judgment for that of the Executive Branch, represented in this case by the Department of Justice. The settled policy is that the courts will not interfere with the executive determination of probable cause for the purpose of filing an Information, in the absence of grave abuse of discretion. That abuse of discretion must be so patent and gross as to amount to an evasion of a positive duty or a virtual refusal to perform a duty enjoined by law or to act at all in contemplation of law, such as where the power is exercised in an arbitrary and despotic manner by reason of passion or hostility.

People); the complaint failed for lack of proof, not immunity. **C is wrong:** the ethics committee's certification was only part of the evidence; the courts decide liability. **Bar trap:** proof of injury is not proof of negligence.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: During an operation, Dr. Lim, the lead surgeon, called in Dr. Santos to remove a growth in another organ. Dr. Santos finished, Dr. Lim examined the work and found it in order, and Dr. Santos left the hospital. As Dr. Lim was finishing, the nurses told him a sponge was missing; a search failed, and Dr. Lim ordered the incision closed. The sponge was later found inside the patient. The patient sues both surgeons and invokes res ipsa loquitur against Dr. Santos, arguing that a sponge left in her body is prima facie proof that every operating surgeon was negligent. Is Dr. Santos liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Res ipsa loquitur does not apply to Dr. Santos, because the thing that caused the injury was not under his control and management; it was under Dr. Lim's, the lead surgeon.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: The requisites of res ipsa loquitur are: the occurrence of an injury; the thing that caused it was under the control and management of the defendant; the occurrence would not ordinarily happen if those in control used proper care; and the absence of explanation by the defendant. The most instrumental is control and management. Under the Captain of the Ship rule, the operating surgeon is the person in complete charge of the surgery room and all personnel connected with the operation, whose duty is to obey his orders. Res ipsa loquitur is also only an evidentiary rule; it does not dispense with proof of negligence. (Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana.)
suggestedAnswer.application: Dr. Lim acted as captain of the ship: he called in Dr. Santos, checked his work, allowed him to leave, and ordered the incision closed even though a sponge was unaccounted for. That order caused the injury, and it was made after Dr. Santos had left. Control and management of what caused the injury was therefore with Dr. Lim, not Dr. Santos.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Dr. Santos is not liable; Dr. Lim is. **Bar trap:** a sponge left inside a patient is prima facie negligence of the operating surgeon in control, not of every doctor who took part in the operation.

keyPoints: Requisites of res ipsa loquitur, with control and management as the most instrumental
Captain of the Ship rule: the lead surgeon is in complete charge of the operating room and its personnel
The lead surgeon's order to close despite the missing sponge caused the injury, after the other surgeon had left
Res ipsa loquitur is only an evidentiary rule and does not replace proof of negligence

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana
source.part: II - G.R. No. 126467 (res ipsa loquitur and the Captain of the Ship rule)
source.excerpt: We find the element of "control and management of the thing which caused the injury" to be wanting. Hence, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur will not lie. It was duly established that Dr. Ampil was the lead surgeon during the operation of Natividad. He requested the assistance of Dr. Fuentes only to perform hysterectomy when he (Dr. Ampil) found that the malignancy in her sigmoid area had spread to her left ovary. Dr. Fuentes performed the surgery and thereafter reported and showed his work to Dr. Ampil. The latter examined it and finding everything to be in order, allowed Dr. Fuentes to leave the operating room. Dr. Ampil then resumed operating on Natividad. He was about to finish the procedure when the attending nurses informed him that two pieces of gauze were missing. A "diligent search" was conducted, but the misplaced gauzes were not found. Dr. Ampil then directed that the incision be closed. During this entire period, Dr. Fuentes was no longer in the operating room and had, in fact, left the hospital. Under the "Captain of the Ship" rule, the operating surgeon is the person in complete charge of the surgery room and all personnel connected with the operation. Their duty is to obey his orders. … Clearly, the control and management of the thing which caused the injury was in the hands of Dr. Ampil, not Dr. Fuentes. In this jurisdiction, res ipsa loquitur is not a rule of substantive law, hence, does not per se create or constitute an independent or separate ground of liability, being a mere evidentiary rule.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A surgeon argues that he cannot be faulted for a sponge left inside his patient, because the patient's life was in danger and a longer search for the missing sponge would have put her at greater risk. Discuss the surgeon's duties with respect to sponges or other foreign objects left in a patient's body.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The surgeon has two duties: to remove all sponges before closing the incision, and, if urgent necessity compels him to leave one, to inform the patient within a reasonable time. Danger to the patient's life may excuse the first but never the second.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, the Court held that an operation requiring sponges is not complete until they are properly removed, and that leaving sponges or other foreign substances in the wound after closing the incision is at least prima facie negligence by the operating surgeon (and, by many authorities, negligence per se). Even when the urgent necessities of the case require a surgeon to leave a sponge because of the dangers of delay, it is his legal duty to inform the patient within a reasonable time of what he had been compelled to do, so that she may seek relief from the effects of the foreign object.
suggestedAnswer.application: The surgeon's emergency may explain why the sponge stayed in, but he must still tell the patient. In Agana, the surgeon closed the incision despite the nurses' report of two missing gauzes, told the patient nothing, and attributed her pain to the operation; the Court held that his initial negligence ripened into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving his patient.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The emergency defense is incomplete: the surgeon remains liable if he fails to disclose the sponge. **Bar trap:** the emergency exception excuses only leaving the sponge, never hiding it from the patient.

keyPoints: An operation is not complete until the sponges are properly removed
Leaving a sponge after closing is at least prima facie negligence of the operating surgeon (negligence per se by many authorities)
Urgent necessity may justify leaving it, but the surgeon must inform the patient within a reasonable time
Concealment turned the surgeon's negligence into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving the patient

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana
source.part: I - G.R. No. 127590 (the surgeon's duties as to sponges left in the body)
source.excerpt: An operation requiring the placing of sponges in the incision is not complete until the sponges are properly removed, and it is settled that the leaving of sponges or other foreign substances in the wound after the incision has been closed is at least prima facie negligence by the operating surgeon. To put it simply, such act is considered so inconsistent with due care as to raise an inference of negligence. There are even legions of authorities to the effect that such act is negligence per se. Of course, the Court is not blind to the reality that there are times when danger to a patient’s life precludes a surgeon from further searching missing sponges or foreign objects left in the body. But this does not leave him free from any obligation. Even if it has been shown that a surgeon was required by the urgent necessities of the case to leave a sponge in his patient’s abdomen, because of the dangers attendant upon delay, still, it is his legal duty to so inform his patient within a reasonable time thereafter by advising her of what he had been compelled to do. This is in order that she might seek relief from the effects of the foreign object left in her body as her condition might permit. … To our mind, what was initially an act of negligence by Dr. Ampil has ripened into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving his patient.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish apparent authority from corporate negligence as grounds for holding a hospital liable for injury to a patient treated by a consultant who is not its employee.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Under apparent authority, the hospital is held liable for the doctor's negligence because it held the doctor out as its agent; under corporate negligence, the hospital is held liable for its own negligence in performing its duties as a hospital.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana (2007), the Court explained that apparent authority (the "holding out" theory, ostensible agency or agency by estoppel) imposes liability not because of a real contractual relationship but because the principal misled the public into believing that the relationship or authority exists; a hospital that holds out a physician as its agent or employee is liable when a patient accepts treatment in the reasonable belief that it is rendered on the hospital's behalf (see Article 1869 of the Civil Code on implied agency). Corporate negligence is the judicial answer to hospital liability absent facts supporting respondeat superior or apparent authority; hospitals have duties such as (1) reasonable care in maintaining safe and adequate facilities and equipment, (2) selecting and retaining competent physicians, (3) overseeing or supervising all persons who practice medicine within their walls, and (4) formulating, adopting and enforcing adequate rules and policies that ensure quality care.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Agana, PSI was liable under apparent authority because it listed Dr. Ampil and Dr. Fuentes in its lobby directory as its accredited physicians, leading patients to believe it vouched for them. It was also directly liable for corporate negligence under Article 2176, because it did not investigate its own nurses' report of two missing gauzes, breaching its duty to oversee those who practice within its walls.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Apparent authority makes the hospital answer vicariously for the doctor; corporate negligence makes it answer directly for itself. **Bar trap:** the 2010 en banc resolution in the same case kept both grounds but declared the corporate-negligence liability pro hac vice (for that case only), and rejected an employer-employee relationship.

keyPoints: Apparent authority: liability by estoppel for the doctor's negligence, because the hospital held him out as its agent and the patient reasonably relied
Other names: holding out theory, ostensible agency, agency by estoppel
Corporate negligence: the hospital's direct liability for its own failure in its duties
The hospital's duties: safe facilities; competent physicians; supervision of those practicing within its walls; adequate rules and policies
In PSI, the 2010 resolution kept both grounds, the corporate-negligence ruling pro hac vice

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana
source.part: III - G.R. No. 126297, Whether PSI Is Liable for the Negligence of Dr. Ampil
source.excerpt: Apparent authority, or what is sometimes referred to as the "holding out" theory, or doctrine of ostensible agency or agency by estoppel, has its origin from the law of agency. It imposes liability, not as the result of the reality of a contractual relationship, but rather because of the actions of a principal or an employer in somehow misleading the public into believing that the relationship or the authority exists. … Thus, in cases where it can be shown that a hospital, by its actions, has held out a particular physician as its agent and/or employee and that a patient has accepted treatment from that physician in the reasonable belief that it is being rendered in behalf of the hospital, then the hospital will be liable for the physician’s negligence. … Recent years have seen the doctrine of corporate negligence as the judicial answer to the problem of allocating hospital’s liability for the negligent acts of health practitioners, absent facts to support the application of respondeat superior or apparent authority. … With the passage of time, more duties were expected from hospitals, among them: (1) the use of reasonable care in the maintenance of safe and adequate facilities and equipment; (2) the selection and retention of competent physicians; (3) the overseeing or supervision of all persons who practice medicine within its walls; and (4) the formulation, adoption and enforcement of adequate rules and policies that ensure quality care for its patients.

He tells the patient nothing, and when she later complains of severe pain he says it is a natural result of the surgery. Following Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, how is his conduct characterized?

choices.A: He is not liable, because a surgeon may close the incision when a diligent search for the missing sponges fails.
choices.B: He is liable only if the patient proves through expert testimony that closing the incision fell below the standard of care.
choices.C: His initial negligence ripened into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving his patient, because he had the duty to inform her of the missing sponges.

To our mind, what was initially an act of negligence by Dr. Ampil has ripened into a deliberate wrongful act of deceiving his patient.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana (2007), why was the hospital held solidarily liable with Dr. Ampil?

choices.A: Because, apart from a general denial of responsibility, it failed to prove that it exercised the diligence of a good father of a family in the accreditation and supervision of Dr. Ampil.
choices.B: Because every hospital is solidarily liable with every doctor who operates in its premises.
choices.C: Because the patient's family signed a contract making the hospital a surety of the doctor.
choices.D: Because Dr. Ampil was a salaried employee of the hospital.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court held that PSI, "apart from a general denial of its responsibility, failed to adduce evidence showing that it exercised the diligence of a good father of a family in the accreditation and supervision" of Dr. Ampil, so it failed to discharge its burden under the last paragraph of Article 2180 and was solidarily liable; it was also directly liable for its own corporate negligence. **B is wrong:** there is no automatic liability for every doctor. **C is wrong:** no such contract figured in the case. **D is wrong:** the trial court found that the doctors were consultants, not salaried employees, and the 2010 en banc resolution confirmed that PSI was not Dr. Ampil's employer. **Bar trap:** in the 2010 resolution the Court changed the grounds of PSI's liability (ostensible agency and, pro hac vice, corporate negligence, not respondeat superior); know both rulings.

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana
source.part: III - G.R. No. 126297 (solidary liability)
source.excerpt: Anent the corollary issue of whether PSI is solidarily liable with Dr. Ampil for damages, let it be emphasized that PSI, apart from a general denial of its responsibility, failed to adduce evidence showing that it exercised the diligence of a good father of a family in the accreditation and supervision of the latter. In neglecting to offer such proof, PSI failed to discharge its burden under the last paragraph of Article 2180 cited earlier, and, therefore, must be adjudged solidarily liable with Dr. Ampil. Moreover, as we have discussed, PSI is also directly liable to the Aganas.

questions.prompt: Gloria's husband chose Dr. Uy to operate on her because, he said, Dr. Uy was a well-known surgeon and a staff member of a prominent hospital. Before the surgery, the hospital had Gloria sign a "consent for hospital care" allowing "the medical, nursing and laboratory staff of this hospital" to give the treatments "deemed necessary by the physicians of this hospital." The nurses' record showed a sponge missing after the operation, but the hospital did nothing about it, leaving it to Dr. Uy, who had promised to tell Gloria himself and never did. Sued with Dr. Uy for the sponge left inside Gloria, the hospital argues that Dr. Uy is a mere consultant, not its employee, over whose work it has no control. Is the hospital liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Even if Dr. Uy is not its employee, the hospital is liable for his negligence as its ostensible agent, and directly liable for its own corporate negligence in failing to act on the report of the missing sponge.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana (2010), the Court en banc held that a hospital is vicariously liable under respondeat superior only if an employment relationship exists, decided by the control test. But even without employment, a hospital is vicariously liable under apparent authority when it holds the doctor out as its agent and the patient relies on it (Article 2176 in relation to Articles 1431 and 1869 of the Civil Code); and regardless of its relationship with the doctor, it is directly liable for its own corporate negligence. The hospital's duty to initiate a review of a reported lapse in its operating room is non-delegable.
suggestedAnswer.application: Lack of control defeats only respondeat superior. The husband chose Dr. Uy believing he was a staff member of a prominent hospital, and the hospital's own consent form called him one of "the physicians of this hospital," reinforcing that belief: both factors of apparent authority are present. And the hospital ignored its own staff's record of a missing sponge, passing to Dr. Uy a review it was bound to start itself; that is its own negligence, separate from Dr. Uy's.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The hospital is liable, vicariously as Dr. Uy's ostensible agent and directly for its corporate negligence. **Bar trap:** "he is not our employee" answers only respondeat superior. Note also that the Court declared its ruling in PSI pro hac vice, so check the facts closely before relying on it.

Apparent authority: the hospital's manifestation that the doctor is its agent, and the patient's reasonable reliance on it
The consent form referring to "the physicians of this hospital" reinforced the impression
Corporate negligence: the hospital's own, non-delegable duty to review a reported lapse; a direct liability distinct from the doctor's
In PSI the Court applied ostensible agency and corporate negligence pro hac vice

Enrique looked upon Dr. Ampil not as independent of but as integrally related to Medical City. PSI's acts tended to confirm and reinforce, rather than negate, Enrique's view. … By such statement, PSI virtually reinforced the public impression that Dr. Ampil was a physician of its hospital, rather than one independently practicing in it; that the medications and treatments he prescribed were necessary and desirable; and that the hospital staff was prepared to carry them out. … By its own standard of corporate conduct, PSI's duty to initiate the review was non-delegable.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Explain the "control test" as applied to doctors and hospitals. Under it, was the hospital in Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana the employer of the surgeon, Dr. Ampil?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Under the control test, an employment relationship exists between a physician and a hospital if the hospital controls both the means and the details of the process by which the physician is to accomplish his task. Under it, PSI was not Dr. Ampil's employer, so it was not liable under respondeat superior.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In its 2010 resolution in Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, the Court en banc held that it still employs the control test (citing Calamba Medical Center v. NLRC), that control is a requisite fact to be established by preponderance of evidence before a hospital may be held vicariously liable as employer, and that it is enough for the employer to have the right to wield the power of control, even without actually supervising. It also noted that in Ramos v. Court of Appeals the 1999 finding of an employment relationship between hospital and consultants was reversed in a 2002 resolution.
suggestedAnswer.application: Both the trial court and the Court of Appeals found that the doctors were consultants and independent contractors, not employees of PSI, and the Aganas never questioned that finding. There was insufficient evidence that PSI controlled the means and details of how Dr. Ampil applied his skills in treating Natividad. PSI therefore could not be held vicariously liable as his employer, though it remained liable as his ostensible principal and for its own corporate negligence.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No employer-employee relationship was shown, so respondeat superior did not apply. **Bar trap:** do not rely on the 1999 Ramos pronouncement that an employer-employee relationship "in effect" exists between hospitals and their consultants; it was reversed, and the control test decides.

It is enough that the hospital has the right to wield the power of control
Control must be proved by preponderance of evidence
PSI did not control Dr. Ampil's work, so no respondeat superior
The 1999 Ramos pronouncement on consultants was reversed in 2002

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and Agana (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, the control test and respondeat superior
source.excerpt: First, there existed between PSI and Dr. Ampil an employer-employee relationship as contemplated in the December 29, 1999 decision in Ramos v. Court of Appeals that "for purposes of allocating responsibility in medical negligence cases, an employer-employee relationship exists between hospitals and their consultants." Although the Court in Ramos later issued a Resolution dated April 11, 2002 reversing its earlier finding on the existence of an employment relationship between hospital and doctor, a similar reversal was not warranted in the present case because the defense raised by PSI consisted of a mere general denial of control or responsibility over the actions of Dr. Ampil. … This Court still employs the "control test" to determine the existence of an employer-employee relationship between hospital and doctor. … Under the "control test", an employment relationship exists between a physician and a hospital if the hospital controls both the means and the details of the process by which the physician is to accomplish his task. … For control test to apply, it is not essential for the employer to actually supervise the performance of duties of the employee, it being enough that it has the right to wield the power. … Control as a determinative factor in testing the employer-employee relationship between doctor and hospital under which the hospital could be held vicariously liable to a patient in medical negligence cases is a requisite fact to be established by preponderance of evidence. Here, there was insufficient evidence that PSI exercised the power of control or wielded such power over the means and the details of the specific process by which Dr. Ampil applied his skills in the treatment of Natividad. Consequently, PSI cannot be held vicariously liable for the negligence of Dr. Ampil under the principle of respondeat superior.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A hospital argues that it cannot be liable for corporate negligence because the surgeon, as captain of the ship, had personally promised to tell the patient about the missing gauzes, and the patient never complained to the hospital. Distinguish corporate negligence from medical negligence, and decide whether the argument is valid.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The argument is not valid. Corporate negligence is the hospital's own failure to perform its duties as a hospital corporation, distinct from the medical negligence of the doctor; the hospital's duty to initiate a review of the missing gauzes was its own and non-delegable.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In the 2010 resolution in Professional Services, Inc. v. Agana, the Court held that the corporate negligence ascribed to PSI is different from the medical negligence attributed to Dr. Ampil: the duties of the hospital are distinct from those of the doctor-consultant, so PSI's failure to fulfill its duties as a hospital gave rise to a direct liability distinct from Dr. Ampil's. PSI's duty to initiate the review was non-delegable; it also had the duty to take notice of medical records prepared by its own staff, especially those bearing earmarks of a surgery gone awry.
suggestedAnswer.application: The surgeon's duty (to tell the patient what happened) and the hospital's duty (to find out when, how and by whom the gauzes were mislaid and to take corrective measures) have different purposes. The surgeon's promise did not relieve the hospital of its own, separate responsibility, and the operation record reporting the gauze count discrepancy should have prompted a review without waiting for the patient to complain.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The hospital is directly liable for its corporate negligence. **Bar trap:** "the doctor was in charge" (captain of the ship) answers the doctor's liability, not the hospital's own; the Court applied this pro hac vice in PSI, based partly on PSI's own judicial admissions.

The hospital's liability for corporate negligence is direct and distinct from the doctor's
The duty to initiate a review of a reported lapse is non-delegable
The hospital must take notice of medical records prepared by its own staff; it should not wait for the patient to complain
PSI's liability was declared pro hac vice

source.caseTitle: Professional Services, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and Agana (Resolution)
source.part: Resolution, corporate negligence
source.excerpt: By its own standard of corporate conduct, PSI's duty to initiate the review was non-delegable. While Dr. Ampil may have had the primary responsibility of notifying Natividad about the missing gauzes, PSI imposed upon itself the separate and independent responsibility of initiating the inquiry into the missing gauzes. The purpose of the first would have been to apprise Natividad of what transpired during her surgery, while the purpose of the second would have been to pinpoint any lapse in procedure that led to the gauze count discrepancy, so as to prevent a recurrence thereof and to determine corrective measures that would ensure the safety of Natividad. That Dr. Ampil negligently failed to notify Natividad did not release PSI from its self-imposed separate responsibility. Corollary to its non-delegable undertaking to review potential incidents of negligence committed within its premises, PSI had the duty to take notice of medical records prepared by its own staff and submitted to its custody, especially when these bear earmarks of a surgery gone awry. Thus, the record taken during the operation of Natividad which reported a gauze count discrepancy should have given PSI sufficient reason to initiate a review. It should not have waited for Natividad to complain. … It should be borne in mind that the corporate negligence ascribed to PSI is different from the medical negligence attributed to Dr. Ampil. The duties of the hospital are distinct from those of the doctor-consultant practicing within its premises in relation to the patient; hence, the failure of PSI to fulfill its duties as a hospital corporation gave rise to a direct liability to the Aganas distinct from that of Dr. Ampil.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Liza, in her fourth pregnancy and with a previous cesarean delivery, was admitted at 31 weeks with bleeding and premature contractions. Her obstetrician gave medicine to delay delivery and relied on an ultrasound taken five weeks earlier, which showed nothing abnormal; no new ultrasound or MRI was ordered, and no blood was reserved for her rare blood type, although the bleeding and contractions stayed minimal for about 16 hours. The next afternoon Liza bled massively; an emergency cesarean and hysterectomy revealed a placenta grown into the uterine wall, and she died before blood arrived. In the heirs' suit, the doctor's expert testifies that he would have done exactly what she did, and the doctor argues that the heirs presented no expert of their own. Is the doctor liable? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The doctor was negligent in failing to anticipate the complications of a high-risk pregnancy: she did not order a timely ultrasound or MRI and did not prepare blood in advance, and timely diagnosis could have prevented the death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Medical negligence requires duty, breach, injury and proximate causation, usually proved through expert witnesses. In Allarey v. Dela Cruz, the Court held that the plaintiffs' failure to present an expert does not bar recovery when the testimony of the defendant physician's own expert establishes the standard of care and supports the plaintiffs' claim, albeit indirectly. A physician exercising the degree of care, skill and diligence in the same field should have considered and anticipated the common complications of preterm labor in a high-risk patient.
suggestedAnswer.application: Liza's history (fourth pregnancy, previous cesarean) and her bleeding with premature contractions made her pregnancy high-risk. The defense expert's own testimony showed that ultrasound and MRI help diagnose placenta accreta, yet none was ordered during the 16 calm hours, and the doctor relied on an outdated ultrasound. His statement that he would have acted the same refers only to the emergency cesarean and hysterectomy, which were proper once the bleeding could no longer be controlled; it does not cover the earlier failure to diagnose and to secure blood of a rare type. Had the condition been diagnosed early, the surgery could have been done before the bleeding became uncontrollable.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The doctor is liable for damages. **Bar trap:** "the plaintiffs presented no expert" is not always fatal, and "my expert would have done the same" must be read for what part of the treatment it covers; correct emergency surgery does not cure negligence in the hours before it.

Timely diagnosis could have averted the deaths (proximate cause)

source.excerpt: From the foregoing, it is clear that the condition of Marissa at the time she was admitted to the hospital, though not normal, is a common complication of preterm labor which a physician exercising the degree of care, skill, and diligence in the same field of practice should have considered and anticipated. … Moreover, the conclusion of Dr. Cardozo that he would have acted the same way as Dr. Dela Cruz did under the same circumstances should not be construed to mean that she was not negligent in treating Marissa during the period leading up to the sudden deterioration of her condition at 1:00 p.m. on August 29, 2006. The context of his conclusion should be construed to mean that what he was referring to was the emergency cesarean operation and hysterectomy conducted on Marissa which are, concededly, the standard of care necessary when bleeding could no longer be controlled or her condition at 1:00 p.m. on August 29, 2006. … Timely and proper diagnosis of Marissa's condition could have prevented or mitigated the severe complications she suffered that led to her and her baby's death. … Furthermore, given the fact that there was at least a period of 16 hours from the time Dr. Dela Cruz physically examined Marissa and the time she experienced profuse bleeding again the next day, Dr. Dela Cruz and the hospital should have already started sourcing blood supply that may be needed by the patient in case of emergency, especially since her blood type is rare.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In what kind of medical negligence cases does the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur apply? Does it apply where the actual cause of the patient's injury has already been identified? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: It applies only in exceptional circumstances, where the failure to observe due care that caused the injury is readily apparent to a layman and is within the exclusive control of the erring physician. It does not apply where the actual cause of the injury has been identified or established.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Allarey v. Dela Cruz, the Court, reviewing its medical negligence cases, held that res ipsa loquitur is applied only in such exceptional circumstances. It cited Cantre v. Spouses Go, where a gaping wound on the patient's arm was not an ordinary occurrence in delivering a baby and could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere; and Borromeo v. Family Care Hospital, which held that the doctrine does not apply to cases where the actual cause of the injury had been identified or established. Its requisites are an accident that ordinarily does not occur without negligence, an instrumentality within the defendant's exclusive control, and no contributing conduct of the plaintiff; control of the instrumentality is the fundamental element.
suggestedAnswer.application: In Allarey, the cause of death was identified: hypovolemic shock from placenta accreta, a condition in which the placenta attaches too deeply into the uterine wall. It was not immediately apparent, often not immediately diagnosed, and arose from the pregnancy itself, not from anything within the doctor's exclusive control. So the doctrine could not apply, and expert testimony was needed to fix the standard of care.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Res ipsa loquitur is exceptional and does not apply once the actual cause is known. **Bar trap:** the doctor in Allarey was still held negligent through the evidence, including her own expert's testimony; the doctrine's failure does not end the case.

Example: a gaping wound on the arm after a delivery (Cantre v. Spouses Go)
Does not apply where the actual cause of the injury is identified or established (Borromeo)
Placenta accreta: not immediately apparent, often not immediately diagnosed, arose from the pregnancy, not under the doctor's exclusive control

source.excerpt: A review of medical negligence cases brought to this Court reveals that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is applied only to exceptional circumstances where the failure to observe due care which caused injury to the patient is readily apparent to a layman and is within the exclusive control of the erring physician. In Cantre v. Spouses Go, the Court applied the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur to justify declaring the physician liable. The Court explained that the gaping wound on the patient's arm is not an ordinary occurrence in the act of delivering a baby and that such "injury could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere." In Borromeo v. Family Care Hospital, Inc., the Court explained that the application of the doctrine "require[s] expert opinion to establish the culpability of the defendant doctor." It also does not apply to cases where the actual cause of the injury had been identified or established. … Placenta accreta is not the contemplated scenario to justify the application of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur as this kind of complication in childbirth is not immediately apparent and, often times, not immediately diagnosed. Here, the medical condition of Marissa was not within the exclusive control of Dr. Dela Cruz.

Dela Cruz, the Court held that in medical negligence cases the four elements (duty, breach, injury and proximate causation) are generally established through expert witnesses, but this rule should not be strictly interpreted to mean that failure to present any expert witness bars recovery. An exception is recognized when the testimony of the expert presented by the defendant physician establishes the standard of care under the circumstances and supports the plaintiffs' claim, albeit indirectly. The loss of the plaintiffs' own expert does not preclude the Court from deciding on the overall evidence.

Read with the medical records, his testimony showed that the doctor should have ordered a timely diagnosis and prepared blood for a high-risk patient, which she did not do. The heirs could rely on that testimony.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, Dr. Dela Cruz and MEMCI were negligent (the plaintiffs' lack of an expert)
source.excerpt: In medical negligence cases, there are four elements that must be established: (1) duty; (2) breach; (3) injury; and (4) proximate causation. In litigations involving medical negligence, the plaintiffs have the burden of establishing these elements through the testimonies of expert witnesses. However, this rule should not be strictly interpreted to mean that the failure to present any expert witness on the part of the plaintiffs shall bar them from recovering damages. An exception that should be recognized such as when the testimony of the expert witness presented by the purported erring defendant physician establishes the standard of care necessary under the given circumstances and supports the claim of the plaintiffs, albeit indirectly. Admittedly, petitioners, who are the plaintiffs in the complaint for quasi-delict, failed to completely present their lone expert witness to substantiate their claim against Dr. Dela Cruz and MEMCI. Dr. Bausa failed to attend several settings for her cross-examination. Nonetheless, this fact alone does not preclude the Court from making its own determination of the rights and liabilities based on the overall evidence presented during trial. This is particularly true when a careful analysis of the testimony of the expert witness presented for the purported erring physician and hospital reveals that it indirectly corroborates the claim of the heirs of Marissa.

choices.B: Yes, because under apparent authority the hospital's representation need not be express; by letting the doctor use its facilities and direct its staff, it impliedly held her out as a member of its medical staff.
choices.C: No, because without an employer-employee relationship a hospital can never be vicariously liable under Article 2180.
choices.D: Yes, because every hospital is an insurer of the results of every procedure done within its premises.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court held MEMCI vicariously liable even though Dr. Dela Cruz was only a consultant, because under apparent authority "the hospital need not make express representations to the patient that the treating physician is an employee of the hospital; rather a representation may be general and implied." Allowing her to use its facilities, instruct its nurses, gather the medical team and refer the patient to its urologist and cardiologist gave the impression that she was a member of its medical staff. **A is wrong:** the Court acknowledged that the prenatal check-ups were done at her own clinic, and still found an implied holding out at the hospital. **C is wrong:** the Court said the absence of an employer-employee relationship "cannot automatically excuse the hospital from any liability." **D is wrong:** the hospital was liable because of the doctor's proven negligence and its holding out, not as an insurer of results; the Court's lower-court rulings even stressed that physicians are not guarantors of results. **Bar trap:** "we never said she was our employee" fails when the hospital's conduct implies it.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, MEMCI is vicariously liable for the negligence of Dr. Dela Cruz
source.excerpt: Admittedly, Dr. Dela Cruz is just a consultant or guest doctor of MEMCI. Nevertheless, even if there is no employer-employee relationship between her and the hospital, this cannot automatically excuse the hospital from any liability. When the doctrine of apparent authority is adopted in medical negligence cases, "the hospital need not make express representations to the patient that the treating physician is an employee of the hospital; rather a representation may be general and implied." In the present case, though all prenatal check-ups of Marissa were conducted at the lying-in clinic of Dr. Dela Cruz outside MEMCI, the hospital impliedly held her out as a member of its medical staff by allowing her to use its facilities to treat her patients. Dr. Dela Cruz gave instructions to the nurse on duty of MEMCI and personally gathered the medical team for the procedures to be performed on Marissa. She even referred Marissa's condition to a urologist and cardiologist-internist while undergoing emergency cesarean section and hysterectomy. All these acts, when taken together, give the impression that she is a member of the medical staff of MEMCI. Thus, MEMCI cannot repudiate now this authority.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A mother dies of massive bleeding during childbirth caused by placenta accreta, a condition in which the placenta attaches too deeply into the uterine wall. Her heirs invoke res ipsa loquitur so they need not present an expert. Following Allarey v. Dela Cruz, will the doctrine apply?

choices.A: No, because placenta accreta is not immediately apparent and often not immediately diagnosed, and it arose from the pregnancy itself rather than from something within the doctor's exclusive control.
choices.B: Yes, because a mother does not ordinarily die in childbirth unless someone was negligent.
choices.C: Yes, because the mother was in the operating room, under the exclusive control of the doctor, when she died.
choices.D: No, because res ipsa loquitur cannot be invoked in an action for damages based on quasi-delict.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court held that placenta accreta "is not the contemplated scenario to justify the application of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur as this kind of complication in childbirth is not immediately apparent and, often times, not immediately diagnosed," and that Marissa's condition was not within the exclusive control of Dr. Dela Cruz, since it arose from the pregnancy itself; so expert testimony had to be resorted to. **B is wrong:** death from a recognized childbirth complication is not something a layman can say happens only through negligence. **C is wrong:** being in the operating room does not put the underlying condition under the doctor's exclusive control. **D is wrong:** the case was itself a quasi-delict action, and the Court examined the requisites on the facts; it did not say the doctrine is unavailable in such actions. **Bar trap:** even where the doctor is ultimately found negligent (as here), res ipsa loquitur may still not apply; the two questions are separate.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur cannot be applied to the present case
source.excerpt: Placenta accreta is not the contemplated scenario to justify the application of the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur as this kind of complication in childbirth is not immediately apparent and, often times, not immediately diagnosed. Here, the medical condition of Marissa was not within the exclusive control of Dr. Dela Cruz. … Accordingly, the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur cannot be applied and expert testimony must be resorted to in order to accurately determine the standard of care necessary for Marissa's condition.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In Allarey v. Dela Cruz, the obstetrician correctly performed an emergency cesarean section and hysterectomy, yet the Court found her negligent. In what did her negligence consist?

choices.A: In performing a hysterectomy without the written consent of the patient's husband.
choices.B: In operating on the patient in a hospital where she was only a consultant.
choices.C: In failing, despite the patient's high-risk history and bleeding, to order a timely ultrasound or MRI during the hours of relative calm and to prepare the blood the patient would likely need.
choices.D: In giving medication to delay delivery, which is never proper in preterm labor.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court held that Dr. Dela Cruz underestimated a high-risk pregnancy (fourth pregnancy, previous cesarean, bleeding with premature contractions), relied on an ultrasound taken more than a month earlier, did not order an ultrasound or MRI though there was minimal bleeding for many hours, and did not start sourcing blood of the patient's rare type during at least 16 hours; timely diagnosis could have prevented or mitigated the complications. **A is wrong:** consent was not the ground of liability. **B is wrong:** being a consultant affects the hospital's liability, not whether the doctor was negligent. **D is wrong:** the Court described tocolysis as the immediate treatment for the contractions; the fault was that there were no efforts to determine the cause of the bleeding. **Bar trap:** proper emergency surgery does not cure negligence in the hours before it.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, Dr. Dela Cruz and MEMCI were negligent
source.excerpt: Instead of addressing the bleeding, she downplayed its seriousness despite knowledge of her medical background and the presence of factors that made her pregnancy high-risk. This was her fourth pregnancy, had three previous deliveries, and her last childbirth delivery was through cesarean section, giving her a higher probability of having placenta accreta or previa. She relied on an ultrasound report prepared more than a month before the patient complained of premature contractions and bleeding. … Noticeably, Dr. Dela Cruz admitted that there were minimal bleeding and contraction between 8:30 pm of August 28, 2006 and 1:00 pm the next day. During this period, Dr. Dela Cruz could have ordered Marissa's ultrasound or MRI yet she did not give such instruction. Timely and proper diagnosis of Marissa's condition could have prevented or mitigated the severe complications she suffered that led to her and her baby's death. … Furthermore, given the fact that there was at least a period of 16 hours from the time Dr. Dela Cruz physically examined Marissa and the time she experienced profuse bleeding again the next day, Dr. Dela Cruz and the hospital should have already started sourcing blood supply that may be needed by the patient in case of emergency, especially since her blood type is rare.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The defense expert in Allarey v. Dela Cruz testified that he would have acted the same way as the defendant obstetrician did under the same circumstances. How did the Court read this testimony?

choices.A: As conclusive proof that the obstetrician met the standard of care throughout the patient's confinement.
choices.B: As inadmissible, because an expert may not compare himself with the defendant.
choices.C: As binding on the heirs, because they failed to present an expert of their own.
choices.D: As referring only to the emergency cesarean and hysterectomy, which were the standard of care once the bleeding could no longer be controlled, not to the care before that point.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that the expert's conclusion "should not be construed to mean that she was not negligent in treating Marissa during the period leading up to the sudden deterioration of her condition"; it referred to the emergency cesarean operation and hysterectomy, which were concededly the standard of care when bleeding could no longer be controlled. **A is wrong:** that is the reading the Court rejected. **B is wrong:** the Court did not exclude the testimony; it read it in context and even used parts of it against the defendant. **C is wrong:** the lack of the heirs' own expert did not bind them to the defense expert's conclusions; the Court weighed all the evidence. **Bar trap:** ask which part of the treatment an expert's approval covers.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, Dr. Dela Cruz and MEMCI were negligent (reading the defense expert's testimony)
source.excerpt: Moreover, the conclusion of Dr. Cardozo that he would have acted the same way as Dr. Dela Cruz did under the same circumstances should not be construed to mean that she was not negligent in treating Marissa during the period leading up to the sudden deterioration of her condition at 1:00 p.m. on August 29, 2006. The context of his conclusion should be construed to mean that what he was referring to was the emergency cesarean operation and hysterectomy conducted on Marissa which are, concededly, the standard of care necessary when bleeding could no longer be controlled or her condition at 1:00 p.m. on August 29, 2006.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Based on the cases discussed in Allarey v. Dela Cruz, in which situation was res ipsa loquitur applied to hold a physician liable?

choices.A: A mother who died of placenta accreta, a complication arising from the pregnancy itself.
choices.B: A patient whose actual cause of injury had already been identified and established.
choices.C: A mother who, after delivering a baby, was found with a gaping wound on her arm, an injury that could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere.
choices.D: A patient whose death required expert opinion to connect it to the treatment.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court cited Cantre v. Spouses Go, where res ipsa loquitur was applied because a gaping wound on the patient's arm is not an ordinary occurrence in delivering a baby, and such "injury could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere." **A is wrong:** that is Allarey itself, where the doctrine was held inapplicable. **B is wrong:** Borromeo holds the doctrine does not apply where the actual cause had been identified or established. **D is wrong:** where expert opinion is needed to link the injury to the treatment, the doctrine, which rests on common knowledge, does not fit. **Bar trap:** the doctrine fits injuries a layman can judge, not complications that need a specialist to explain.

source.caseTitle: Allarey, et al. v. Dela Cruz and Manila East Medical Center, Inc.
source.part: Ruling of the Court, The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur cannot be applied (citing Cantre and Borromeo)
source.excerpt: A review of medical negligence cases brought to this Court reveals that the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur is applied only to exceptional circumstances where the failure to observe due care which caused injury to the patient is readily apparent to a layman and is within the exclusive control of the erring physician. In Cantre v. Spouses Go, the Court applied the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur to justify declaring the physician liable. The Court explained that the gaping wound on the patient's arm is not an ordinary occurrence in the act of delivering a baby and that such "injury could not have happened unless negligence had set in somewhere." In Borromeo v. Family Care Hospital, Inc., the Court explained that the application of the doctrine "require[s] expert opinion to establish the culpability of the defendant doctor." It also does not apply to cases where the actual cause of the injury had been identified or established.
